lotteries.justification: Shape: is the reward willing to gamble a certain success away for speed? C = T002 (824.32), a certain gently-gripped success ending 94% open. Good branch A = T253 (1064.32), a fast hook-and-hold success. Bad branch B = T239 (329.63), random flailing that never touches the drawer. p* = (824.32 - 329.63)/(1064.32 - 329.63) = 0.6733. I set p = 0.69, just onto the lottery-preferring side: the gamble is worth 0.69*1064.32 + 0.31*329.63 = 836.6 against C's 824.3 — a definite but small margin of 12 points (1.5%). That is exactly the hard p: the designed reward accepts a 31% chance the drawer is never touched at all, rather than take a certain successful open, in exchange for a chance at a faster one. A person who cares whether the drawer ends up open would take C without hesitating.

lotteries.justification: Different shape: the bad branch is not failure-to-act but the agent undoing its own work, and here NO p can make the reward prefer the certain trajectory. C = T004 (810.81), a certain gently-gripped success ending 88% open. Good branch A = T256 (1064.31), a fast success. Bad branch B = T045 (936.20), a run that opens the drawer to 88% and then shoves it fully shut, ending 0% open. Because even the bad branch out-scores the certain success, p* = (810.81 - 936.20)/(1064.31 - 936.20) = -0.98 lies outside [0,1] — the reward prefers the lottery at every p. I chose p = 0.05 to make that maximally legible: even when the gamble ends with the drawer shoved shut 95% of the time, the reward still prefers it (942.6 vs 810.8) over a certain successful open. The question for the human is how low a success probability they would tolerate; the reward's answer is zero.
